hints: Resolve forces perpendicular to the incline to find the normal reaction $R = mg\cos\theta$ with $m = 1.3\text{ kg}$ and $g = 10\text{ m s}^{-2}$.
Because the particle is on the point of moving up the plane, the limiting friction force $F = \mu R$ acts down the plane.
Resolve forces parallel to the plane: equate the upward applied force $20\text{ N}$ to $mg\sin\theta + F$, then solve for $\mu$.
walkthrough:
Find the trigonometric ratios for $\theta$ from $\tan\theta = \frac{12}{5}$:
$$\cos\theta = \frac{5}{13}, \quad \sin\theta = \frac{12}{13}$$

Resolve forces perpendicular to the inclined plane to determine the normal reaction force $R$ with $m = 1.3\text{ kg}$ and $g = 10\text{ m s}^{-2}$:
$$R = mg\cos\theta = 1.3(10)\left(\frac{5}{13}\right) = 13\left(\frac{5}{13}\right) = 5\text{ N}$$

Resolve forces parallel to the plane in limiting equilibrium with impending upward motion, so friction $F$ acts downwards:
$$20 = mg\sin\theta + F$$
$$20 = 13\left(\frac{12}{13}\right) + F = 12 + F$$
$$F = 20 - 12 = 8\text{ N}$$

Apply the limiting friction formula $F = \mu R$ to solve for $\mu$:
$$\mu = \frac{F}{R} = \frac{8}{5} = 1.6$$
teacher_walkthrough:
Find $\sin\theta$ and $\cos\theta$ from $\tan\theta = \frac{12}{5}$. In a right-angled triangle with opposite side $12$ and adjacent side $5$, the hypotenuse is $\sqrt{12^2 + 5^2} = 13$:
$$\sin\theta = \frac{12}{13}, \quad \cos\theta = \frac{5}{13}$$

The weight of the particle is $W = mg = 1.3 \times 10 = 13\text{ N}$. Resolve perpendicular to the inclined plane in equilibrium:
$$R - mg\cos\theta = 0$$
$$R = mg\cos\theta = 13 \times \frac{5}{13} = 5\text{ N}$$

The particle is on the point of slipping up the plane, so limiting friction $F$ acts down the plane to oppose impending motion. Resolve parallel to the plane in equilibrium:
$$\sum F_{\parallel} = 0$$
$$20 - mg\sin\theta - F = 0$$
Substitute $mg\sin\theta = 13 \times \frac{12}{13} = 12\text{ N}$:
$$20 - 12 - F = 0$$
$$8 - F = 0$$
$$F = 8\text{ N}$$

State the limiting friction law relating friction, normal reaction, and coefficient of friction:
$$F = \mu R$$
Substitute $F = 8\text{ N}$ and $R = 5\text{ N}$:
$$8 = \mu \times 5$$
Divide by $5$:
$$\mu = \frac{8}{5} = 1.6$$
Thus the coefficient of friction is $1.6$.

hints: When the $20\text{ N}$ pulling force is removed, the downward component of weight is $mg\sin\theta = 12\text{ N}$.
Check whether the particle moves: maximum available friction is $\mu R = 1.6(5) = 8\text{ N}$, which is less than $12\text{ N}$, so the particle accelerates down the plane.
Apply Newton's second law down the plane: $mg\sin\theta - F = ma$, where friction $F = 8\text{ N}$ acts up the plane.
walkthrough:
Identify the forces acting parallel to the plane when the $20\text{ N}$ force is removed: the weight component down the slope is $mg\sin\theta = 12\text{ N}$ and friction opposes motion up the slope with limiting magnitude $F = \mu R = 1.6(5) = 8\text{ N}$:
$$F_{\text{net}} = mg\sin\theta - F = 12 - 8 = 4\text{ N}$$

Apply Newton's second law $F_{\text{net}} = ma$ down the slope with $m = 1.3\text{ kg}$:
$$4 = 1.3a$$
$$a = \frac{4}{1.3} = \frac{40}{13} \approx 3.08\text{ m s}^{-2}$$
teacher_walkthrough:
When the external $20\text{ N}$ force is removed, check the direction of impending or actual motion. The component of weight pulling the particle down the slope is:
$$W_{\parallel} = mg\sin\theta = 1.3 \times 10 \times \frac{12}{13} = 12\text{ N}$$
The maximum friction opposing downward motion is:
$$F_{\max} = \mu R = 1.6 \times 5 = 8\text{ N}$$
Since $12\text{ N} > 8\text{ N}$, the particle must accelerate down the plane, and friction acts up the plane with magnitude $F = 8\text{ N}$.

Apply Newton's second law along the plane in the downward direction:
$$F_{\text{net}} = ma$$
$$mg\sin\theta - F = ma$$
Substitute the known values:
$$12 - 8 = 1.3a$$
$$4 = 1.3a$$

Divide both sides by $1.3$:
$$a = \frac{4}{1.3} = \frac{40}{13} \approx 3.0769\text{ m s}^{-2} \approx 3.08\text{ m s}^{-2}$$
Thus the acceleration is $3.08\text{ m s}^{-2}$ directed down the plane.

hints: Find the distance $s$ moved down the plane during the first $2\text{ s}$ using $s = ut + \frac{1}{2}at^2$ with $u = 0$ and $a = \frac{40}{13}\text{ m s}^{-2}$.
Recall that the friction force during motion is constant with magnitude $F = 8\text{ N}$.
Calculate work done against friction using $W = F \times s$.
walkthrough:
Calculate the distance travelled down the plane in $t = 2\text{ s}$ from rest with acceleration $a = \frac{40}{13}\text{ m s}^{-2}$:
$$s = ut + \frac{1}{2}at^2 = 0 + \frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{40}{13}\right)(2^2) = \frac{80}{13} \approx 6.1538\text{ m}$$

Calculate the work done against friction using $W = F \times s$ with friction force $F = 8\text{ N}$:
$$W = 8 \times \frac{80}{13} = \frac{640}{13} \approx 49.2\text{ J}$$
teacher_walkthrough:
State the constant acceleration equation to determine the distance $s$ travelled down the slope during the first $t = 2\text{ s}$, starting from rest ($u = 0$):
$$s = ut + \frac{1}{2}at^2$$
Substitute $u = 0$, $a = \frac{40}{13}\text{ m s}^{-2}$, and $t = 2\text{ s}$:
$$s = 0 \times 2 + \frac{1}{2} \times \frac{40}{13} \times 2^2$$
$$s = \frac{1}{2} \times \frac{40}{13} \times 4 = \frac{80}{13} \approx 6.1538\text{ m}$$

State the formula for work done against a constant frictional resistance:
$$W = F \times s$$
From part (i) and (ii), the friction force during motion is $F = 8\text{ N}$.

Substitute $F = 8\text{ N}$ and $s = \frac{80}{13}\text{ m}$:
$$W = 8 \times \frac{80}{13} = \frac{640}{13} \approx 49.2308\text{ J} \approx 49.2\text{ J}$$
Thus the work done against friction during the first $2\text{ s}$ of motion is $49.2\text{ J}$.
